questions.title: First level of DNA packing
questions.question: What is the first level of DNA packing in metaphase chromosome?

explanations.A: Incorrect. Euchromatin describes transcriptionally active, loosely packed chromatin at a much higher order of organisation, not the first level of DNA packing.
explanations.B: Incorrect. A gene is a functional unit of DNA sequence, not a level of physical packing at all.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Histones are the proteins that do the packing, but the named first-level packing unit they form is the nucleosome, not the histone protein by itself.
explanations.D: Correct. The nucleosome — a histone octamer (two copies each of H2A, H2B, H3 and H4) wrapped by about 140 bp of DNA, connected to the next nucleosome by H1-bound linker DNA — is the first level of DNA packing, giving chromatin its beads-on-a-string appearance before further, higher-order coiling condenses it into the metaphase chromosome. Because histones are lysine- and arginine-rich basic proteins, they are positively charged and bind the acidic, phosphate-rich DNA electrostatically. This first packing level is what all higher orders of chromatin condensation (30 nm fibre, loops, and finally the metaphase chromosome itself) are built on top of.

questions.subject: fnd
questions.learning_objective: Name the nucleosome as the first level of DNA packing, distinct from euchromatin, a gene, or the histone protein alone.

questions.title: Crossing over and meiotic prophase
questions.question: Crossing over (pachytene) takes place in which phase?

explanations.A: Incorrect. By metaphase, homologous chromosomes are already aligned at the metaphase plate; the exchange of material has already occurred earlier, at prophase.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Anaphase is when homologous chromosomes are actively separating and moving to opposite poles, well after any crossing over has taken place.
explanations.C: Correct. Crossing over — reciprocal exchange of genetic material between paired homologous chromosomes — happens at pachytene, one of five substages of meiosis I prophase (leptotene, zygotene, pachytene, diplotene, diakinesis), after the chromosomes have fully synapsed at zygotene. This reshuffles maternal and paternal alleles between homologous chromosomes before they separate, producing genetic recombination. It is this prophase-stage exchange, not any later stage, that the pachytene substage is specifically named for.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Telophase I is the final stage of the first meiotic division, when the chromosomes have already reached the poles and nuclear envelopes are reforming — long after any crossing over.

questions.subject: fnd
questions.learning_objective: Name pachytene, a substage of meiosis I prophase, as the point at which crossing over occurs.

questions.title: Intermediate filament protein of skin
questions.question: The intermediate filaments found in skin composed of which type of protein?

explanations.A: Incorrect. Tubulin is the subunit protein of microtubules, an entirely different cytoskeletal system, not an intermediate filament protein at all.
explanations.B: Correct. Keratin is the intermediate filament protein of skin (epidermal) epithelium. Keratin filaments anchor to desmosomes and hemidesmosomes, giving epidermal cells the mechanical resilience they need to resist shearing forces from multiple directions. Each intermediate filament type is tissue-specific — keratin marks epithelial cells specifically, distinguishing this cell type on immunohistochemistry.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Vimentin is the intermediate filament protein of mesenchymal-derived cells (fibroblasts, endothelial cells), not epithelium.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Desmin is the intermediate filament protein of muscle cells, not skin epithelium.

questions.subject: fnd
questions.learning_objective: Name keratin as the skin epithelium's intermediate filament protein, distinct from tubulin, vimentin and desmin.

questions.title: Glands that secrete through a duct
questions.question: What type of gland secretes its product through a duct or tube?

explanations.A: Incorrect. Endocrine glands are ductless — secretory cells release their hormone directly into surrounding blood capillaries, not through a duct.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Multicellular is a description of how many cells make up the gland (versus unicellular, like a goblet cell), not a classification based on the presence of a duct.
explanations.C: Correct. Glands are classified by the presence or absence of a duct. An exocrine gland has a secretory portion and an excretory portion — its duct — that carries the secretion outside the gland (to a body surface or lumen). This is distinct from an endocrine gland, which is ductless, and from a mixed gland (like the pancreas), which has both an exocrine, duct-bearing part and an endocrine, ductless part.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Merocrine describes a mode of secretion (exocytosis, with no loss of cell material), not whether the gland has a duct — merocrine glands are a subtype of exocrine gland, not a synonym for having a duct.

questions.subject: fnd
questions.learning_objective: Identify the exocrine gland as the type defined by having a duct, distinct from the ductless endocrine gland and the secretion-mode-based merocrine classification.

questions.title: Striated duct surface specialisation
questions.question: What is the type of epithelial cell specialization found in striated ducts of salivary glands for increasing surface area for transport?

explanations.A: Correct. Basal infoldings of the plasma membrane, with mitochondria stacked vertically between them, increase the basal surface area of striated duct cells to power the active ion transport (Na+ reabsorption) that gives the duct its striated appearance and its name. This basal membrane specialisation is distinct in location and function from apical specialisations.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Microvilli are apical, not basal, surface specialisations that increase absorptive surface area — they characterise cells like enterocytes, not the basal ion-transport machinery of the striated duct.
explanations.C: Incorrect. The basement membrane is a structural anchoring layer beneath the epithelium, not a surface-area-increasing specialisation.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Gap junctions are lateral intercellular channels for direct cell-to-cell communication, unrelated to increasing transport surface area.

questions.subject: fnd
questions.learning_objective: Identify basal infoldings as the striated duct's surface-area-increasing specialisation for active transport, distinct from microvilli, the basement membrane and gap junctions.

questions.title: Classification of pseudostratified epithelium
questions.question: Pseudostratified columnar epithelium belongs to which type of the following?

explanations.A: Correct. Pseudostratified columnar epithelium is classified as simple epithelium, because every one of its cells rests on the basement membrane — it only appears layered because the cells' nuclei sit at different heights, not because there are genuinely multiple cell layers stacked on top of each other. It comes in three forms distinguished by what sits on the apical surface (ciliated, non-ciliated, or with stereocilia).
explanations.B: Incorrect. True stratified epithelium has multiple genuine cell layers, with only the basal layer touching the basement membrane — unlike pseudostratified epithelium, where every cell reaches the basement membrane despite the layered appearance.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Neuro-epithelium is a specialised sensory epithelial type (e.g. olfactory epithelium), a different classification axis entirely from the simple/stratified distinction.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Myoepithelium refers to contractile epithelial cells (found around secretory acini and ducts), not a layering classification.

questions.subject: fnd
questions.learning_objective: Classify pseudostratified columnar epithelium as simple epithelium, since every cell reaches the basement membrane despite its layered appearance.

questions.title: Neutrophil band cell
questions.question: Which of the following characterizes neutrophil?

options.B: Its immature form called band cell.

explanations.A: Incorrect. The mature neutrophil's nucleus is multi-lobed (2 to 5 lobes connected by thin strands), not S-shaped.
explanations.B: Correct. The neutrophil's immature form, released early from the bone marrow under demand such as infection, is called the band cell (band neutrophil) — its nucleus is an unsegmented, curved band rather than the mature cell's multi-lobed nucleus. A rise in circulating band cells, known as a left shift, is a bedside marker of an acute inflammatory or infectious response. This maturation-stage terminology is a core hematology identification fact.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Neutrophils have neutrophilic (faintly staining, not acidophilic) granules — acidophilic (eosinophilic) granules characterise the eosinophil, a different granulocyte.
explanations.D: Incorrect. The neutrophil does contain azurophilic (primary) granules, alongside its specific (secondary) granules — it does not lack them.

questions.subject: hem
questions.learning_objective: Identify the band cell as the neutrophil's immature form, and correctly reject the distractor claims about the mature neutrophil's nucleus shape and granule staining.

questions.title: Origin of platelets
questions.question: Platelets are formed from what type of cell?

explanations.A: Incorrect. Mast cells release histamine and other mediators in allergic/inflammatory responses; they do not give rise to platelets.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Macrophages are phagocytic cells derived from monocytes, an unrelated lineage from platelet production.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Plasma cells are terminally differentiated B lymphocytes that secrete antibodies; they play no role in platelet formation.
explanations.D: Correct. Bone-marrow megakaryocytes produce platelets — large polyploid cells whose cytoplasm is shed as platelet fragments (via demarcation membrane channels and platelet ribbons/pseudopodia) into the circulation. This is one of the most fundamental cell-lineage facts in hematology, and megakaryocytes are recognised on marrow smears by their large size and single multilobed nucleus.

questions.subject: hem
questions.learning_objective: Identify the megakaryocyte as the cell of origin for platelets, distinct from the mast cell, macrophage and plasma cell.

questions.title: Dense irregular connective tissue example
questions.question: Which structure is composed of dense irregular connective tissue?

explanations.A: Incorrect. The tendon is dense regular connective tissue — its collagen fibres run in one parallel direction, to resist force along the single axis of muscle pull.
explanations.B: Correct. The organ capsule (e.g. of the spleen, kidney or liver) is a classic example of dense irregular connective tissue, whose thick collagen bundles run in multiple, interwoven directions, giving it strength to resist stress from many directions at once around an organ's variably-shaped surface. The dermis is another dense irregular connective tissue example.
explanations.C: Incorrect. The lamina propria of mucosa is loose, not dense, connective tissue.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Like the tendon, the ligament is dense regular connective tissue, with parallel collagen fibres along one axis, not the multidirectional arrangement of dense irregular connective tissue.

questions.subject: fnd
questions.learning_objective: Identify the organ capsule as an example of dense irregular connective tissue, distinct from the tendon and ligament (dense regular) and lamina propria (loose connective tissue).

questions.title: Symport across the cell membrane
questions.question: Regarding transport across cell membrane, which of the following is an example of co-transport (Symport)?

explanations.A: Incorrect. Ca2+/Na+ exchange is antiport (countertransport) — the two ions move in opposite directions, not the same direction that defines symport.
explanations.B: Correct. Symport (co-transport) moves two solutes in the same direction, using the downhill electrochemical gradient of one (typically Na+) to drive the uphill movement of the other. The Na+/amino acid carrier is a textbook example, moving both Na+ and the amino acid into the cell together.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Na+/H+ exchange is antiport, moving Na+ in and H+ out — opposite directions, not symport.
explanations.D: Incorrect. The Na+/K+ pump is primary active transport, using ATP hydrolysis directly to move Na+ and K+ in opposite directions across the membrane, not a symporter using another ion's gradient.

questions.subject: fnd
questions.learning_objective: Identify Na+/amino acid cotransport as an example of symport, distinct from the Na+/H+ and Ca2+/Na+ antiporters and the Na+/K+ pump's primary active transport.

questions.title: Fick's law and membrane thickness
questions.question: Regarding diffusion, which of the following is inversely proportionate to the rate of simple diffusion?

explanations.A: Incorrect. The concentration gradient is directly proportional to diffusion rate — a steeper gradient drives faster net diffusion, not slower.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Surface area of the membrane is directly proportional to diffusion rate — more area means more room for molecules to cross per unit time.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Temperature is directly proportional to diffusion rate — higher temperature means more kinetic energy and faster molecular movement.
explanations.D: Correct. By Fick's law, the rate of simple diffusion is inversely proportional to the membrane's thickness — a thicker membrane forces the solute to travel a longer path, slowing diffusion. This is the one factor among the four listed here that reduces, rather than increases, the diffusion rate as it rises.

questions.subject: fnd
questions.learning_objective: Identify membrane thickness as the factor inversely proportional to the rate of simple diffusion, distinct from concentration gradient, surface area and temperature.

questions.title: Secondary active transport and amino acids
questions.question: If secondary active transport is disturbed, transport of which molecules would be impaired?

explanations.A: Incorrect. Urea crosses membranes by simple diffusion (facilitated in some tissues by urea transporters, but not dependent on a Na+-coupled secondary active carrier), so disturbing secondary active transport would not impair it.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Alcohol is small and lipid-soluble enough to cross membranes by simple diffusion, independent of any transporter.
explanations.C: Incorrect. O2 crosses membranes by simple diffusion down its partial-pressure gradient, requiring no transporter at all.
explanations.D: Correct. Amino acid absorption across the gut and renal tubular epithelium depends on secondary active transport — Na+-amino acid symporters that use the Na+ gradient built by the Na+/K+-ATPase to move amino acids uphill without directly consuming ATP themselves. Disturbing secondary active transport would specifically impair amino acid transport, unlike urea, alcohol and O2, which need no transporter at all.

questions.subject: fnd
questions.learning_objective: Identify amino acids as the solute whose transport depends on secondary active transport, distinct from urea, alcohol and O2, which cross by simple diffusion.

questions.title: Sympathetic effects on abdominal organs
questions.question: Stimulation of sympathetic supply to abdominal organs results in which of the following actions?

explanations.A: Correct. Sympathetic stimulation of abdominal organs inhibits intestinal secretions and motility — the opposite of the parasympathetic system's 'rest and digest' effect — redirecting the body's resources toward a 'fight or flight' state.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Sympathetic stimulation inhibits, not stimulates, insulin secretion, acting via alpha-2 adrenergic receptors on pancreatic beta cells.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Sympathetic stimulation promotes glycogenolysis (glycogen breakdown, to raise blood glucose), not glycogenesis (glycogen synthesis), its opposite.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Sympathetic stimulation decreases, not increases, intestinal motility.

questions.subject: fnd
questions.learning_objective: State that sympathetic stimulation inhibits intestinal secretions, and correctly reject the distractors describing increased insulin secretion, glycogenesis or intestinal motility.

questions.title: Vagal effects of the parasympathetic cranial outflow
questions.question: Parasympathetic nervous system has a cranial outflow. Stimulation of the vagus nerve causes which of the following effects?

explanations.A: Incorrect. The vagus nerve, a parasympathetic nerve, slows heart rate (bradycardia); tachycardia is a sympathetic effect.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Mydriasis (pupil dilation) is a sympathetic effect; parasympathetic stimulation instead constricts the pupil (miosis).
explanations.C: Correct. Among the vagus nerve's parasympathetic effects is bronchiolar smooth-muscle contraction, constricting the airway — the opposite of sympathetic bronchodilation. This is a genuine cranial parasympathetic (vagal) effect, unlike the other three options here.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Micturition (bladder detrusor contraction) is driven by the sacral parasympathetic outflow (pelvic splanchnic nerves, S2-S4), a different parasympathetic outflow from the vagus nerve's cranial territory.

questions.subject: fnd
questions.learning_objective: Identify bronchiolar constriction as a genuine vagal (cranial parasympathetic) effect, distinct from tachycardia and mydriasis (sympathetic) and micturition (sacral parasympathetic outflow).

questions.title: Juxtaglomerular cell stimulation
questions.question: Regarding nervous control of body water, which of the following stimulates juxtaglomerular cells of kidney?

explanations.A: Incorrect. Hypervolemia raises renal perfusion pressure, which suppresses, rather than stimulates, renin release from juxtaglomerular (JG) cells.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Hypertension likewise raises renal perfusion pressure, suppressing JG-cell renin release rather than stimulating it.
explanations.C: Correct. Juxtaglomerular cells, modified smooth muscle cells in the afferent arteriole wall, release renin in response to reduced renal perfusion pressure — the state produced by hypovolemia — triggering the renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system to restore blood volume and pressure.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Hyperosmolarity is instead sensed by hypothalamic osmoreceptors, driving ADH release — a different sensor system entirely from the JG cells' pressure/volume sensing.

questions.subject: fnd
questions.learning_objective: Identify hypovolemia as the stimulus for juxtaglomerular cell renin release, distinct from hypervolemia and hypertension (which suppress it) and hyperosmolarity (sensed by a different receptor system).

questions.title: Angiotensin II and ADH secretion
questions.question: Which of the following describes angiotensin II's role in the regulation of body water?

explanations.A: Incorrect. Angiotensin II stimulates, not inhibits, thirst sensation, as part of its overall water-and-sodium-retaining action.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Angiotensin II increases, not decreases, aldosterone secretion from the adrenal cortex.
explanations.C: Correct. Angiotensin II increases ADH (vasopressin) secretion from the posterior pituitary, alongside its other roles of stimulating thirst and raising aldosterone — all coordinated toward retaining water and sodium to restore blood volume and pressure.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Angiotensin II opposes, rather than stimulates, atrial natriuretic peptide, which is released in response to volume expansion — a state angiotensin II's water-retaining actions work against.

questions.subject: fnd
questions.learning_objective: State that angiotensin II increases ADH secretion as part of body-water regulation, and correctly reject the distractors reversing its effects on thirst, aldosterone and ANP.

questions.title: Erythropoiesis and kidney failure
questions.question: Regarding erythropoiesis, which of the following is true?

options.A: Lesion in bone marrow leads to megaloblastic anemia
options.B: Kidney failure leads to depression of bone marrow
options.C: Oxalates, phytate & phosphate increase absorption of iron
options.D: Hypoxia inhibits the secretion of erythropoietin hormone

explanations.A: Incorrect. Megaloblastic anemia is caused by B12 or folate deficiency, a nutritional problem, not a structural marrow lesion, which instead causes aplastic-type marrow failure.
explanations.B: Correct. The kidney is the principal source of erythropoietin, the hormone driving red-cell production in the bone marrow. Kidney failure lowers erythropoietin output, and with it, marrow erythropoiesis — the mechanism behind the anemia of chronic kidney disease. This renal-erythropoietin-marrow axis is the key regulatory link being tested here.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Dietary oxalates and phytates decrease, not increase, intestinal iron absorption, by chelating iron and preventing its uptake.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Hypoxia stimulates, not inhibits, erythropoietin secretion — the opposite of the distractor's claim, and the basis of the physiological response to altitude or chronic lung disease.

questions.subject: hem
questions.learning_objective: State that kidney failure depresses bone marrow erythropoiesis via reduced erythropoietin secretion, and correctly reject the distractors about bone-marrow lesions, oxalate/phytate effects on iron absorption, and hypoxia's effect on erythropoietin.

questions.title: Congenital spherocytosis
questions.question: Which of the following is best describe congenital spherocytosis disease?

options.B: It is regarded as a type of hemolytic anemia
options.C: It is a non-sex-linked Mendelian recessive disease
options.D: In which the cell membrane is more permeable to K+ ion

explanations.A: Incorrect. Hereditary spherocytosis produces spherocytic, microcytic-appearing (not macrocytic) red cells that have lost the normal biconcave disc shape.
explanations.B: Correct. Hereditary spherocytosis produces less-flexible spherical RBCs that hemolyze readily because of membrane-protein mutations (spectrin, ankyrin and related cytoskeletal proteins) — it is regarded as a type of hemolytic anemia, since the abnormal cells are prematurely destroyed, chiefly in the spleen.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Hereditary spherocytosis is most commonly autosomal dominant, not a non-sex-linked recessive disease.
explanations.D: Incorrect. The characteristic membrane defect increases permeability to Na+, not K+, contributing to the cell's fragility and loss of its normal shape.

questions.subject: hem
questions.learning_objective: State that hereditary spherocytosis is a hemolytic anemia caused by RBC membrane-protein defects, and correctly reject the distractors about cell size, inheritance pattern and ion permeability.

questions.title: Adrenaline in bronchial asthma
questions.question: Concerning sympathetic nervous system, which of the following best describe it?

options.A: Stimulation of B3 receptors increases heart rate
options.B: Sympatholytic drugs are used in hemorrhage
options.C: Adrenaline used in treatment of bronchial asthma
options.D: Sympathomimetic drugs are used in angina pectoris

explanations.A: Incorrect. Beta-3 receptor stimulation increases lipolysis and thermogenesis, not heart rate — beta-1 receptors, not beta-3, govern chronotropy (heart rate).
explanations.B: Incorrect. Sympathomimetic, not sympatholytic, drugs are used to support blood pressure in hemorrhage/shock, by raising vascular tone and cardiac output.
explanations.C: Correct. Adrenaline (epinephrine), acting via beta-2 adrenergic receptors, relaxes bronchial smooth muscle and is used to treat acute bronchospasm in bronchial asthma. This beta-2-mediated bronchodilation is a distinct receptor action from adrenaline's beta-1 (heart rate) and beta-3 (metabolic) effects.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Vasodilators, not sympathomimetics, are used in angina pectoris — increasing sympathetic drive would raise myocardial oxygen demand and worsen, not treat, angina.

questions.subject: fnd
questions.learning_objective: State that adrenaline is used to treat bronchial asthma via beta-2-mediated bronchodilation, and correctly reject the distractors about beta-3 receptors and heart rate, sympatholytic drugs in hemorrhage, and sympathomimetic drugs in angina.

questions.title: Stored blood potassium
questions.question: Which of the following occurs in stored blood?

options.C: Increase dextrose and changed to lactic acid
options.D: Increase plasma concentration of tissue factor

explanations.A: Incorrect. 2,3-DPG falls, not rises, during blood storage, impairing the stored red cells' ability to offload oxygen after transfusion.
explanations.B: Correct. During blood storage, red cells slowly lose membrane integrity and leak intracellular potassium into the plasma, so plasma K+ rises the longer blood is stored — a clinically relevant risk in massive or rapid transfusion, especially in neonates or renally impaired patients.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Glucose (dextrose) falls, not rises, during storage, as ongoing red cell glycolysis consumes it and produces lactate — the option's framing reverses the direction of the glucose change.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Stored blood does not show a clinically significant rise in tissue factor as a defining storage-lesion change; this is not one of the recognised storage lesion findings.

questions.subject: hem
questions.learning_objective: State that stored blood shows a rise in plasma potassium, and correctly reject the distractors misstating the direction of 2,3-DPG and glucose changes during storage.

questions.title: Definition of opsonization
questions.question: Regarding opsonization, which of the following best describe it?

options.A: It is the ability of WBCs to migrate through unbroken capillaries
options.B: Is describe as the chemotaxis ability of WBCs
options.C: Making the foreign materials more susceptible for phagocytosis
options.D: Means decreasing number of WBCs below 4000 / mm2

explanations.A: Incorrect. Migration of WBCs through unbroken capillary walls describes diapedesis, not opsonization.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Chemotaxis describes directed WBC movement toward a chemical stimulus (such as bacterial products or complement fragments), a different process from opsonization.
explanations.C: Correct. Opsonization is the process by which IgG antibody and/or the complement fragment C3b coat (tag) a microbial antigen, so that phagocytes bearing Fc receptors or complement receptors recognise the coated particle far more efficiently — making the foreign material more susceptible to phagocytosis. This tagging step is distinct from neutralization, agglutination and other antibody-mediated effector functions.
explanations.D: Incorrect. A WBC count below 4000/mm3 describes leukopenia, an unrelated laboratory finding, not opsonization.

questions.subject: imm
questions.learning_objective: State the definition of opsonization as tagging foreign material for enhanced phagocytosis, distinct from diapedesis, chemotaxis and leukopenia.

questions.title: Lactulose in constipation and hepatic encephalopathy
questions.question: Which of the following disaccharides is used in treatment of constipation and hepatic encephalopathy?

explanations.A: Correct. Lactulose is an unabsorbed synthetic fructose-galactose disaccharide that retains bowel water — giving it an osmotic laxative effect used in constipation — and is metabolized by colonic bacteria to lactic acid, lowering colonic pH and trapping ammonia as the non-absorbable ammonium ion, the mechanism used to treat hepatic encephalopathy.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Sucrose is a normal dietary disaccharide (glucose-fructose) that is digested and absorbed; it has no laxative or ammonia-trapping therapeutic use.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Lactose is the normal dietary disaccharide of milk (glucose-galactose); it is not used therapeutically for constipation or hepatic encephalopathy.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Maltose is a starch-digestion product (two glucose units); it has no role in treating constipation or hepatic encephalopathy.

questions.subject: git
questions.learning_objective: Identify lactulose as the disaccharide used to treat both constipation and hepatic encephalopathy, distinct from sucrose, lactose and maltose.

questions.title: Essential fatty acid
questions.question: Fatty acid can be classified into essential and non-essential. Which of the following is an essential fatty acid?

explanations.A: Incorrect. Oleic acid is a non-essential fatty acid — the body synthesizes it readily.
explanations.B: Correct. Linoleic acid, an omega-6 polyunsaturated fatty acid, is essential — the body cannot synthesize it de novo and must obtain it from the diet.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Arachidonic acid, while biologically important as an eicosanoid precursor, is only conditionally essential: it can be synthesized from linoleic acid itself when dietary linoleic acid is adequate, so it is not a true dietary essential fatty acid in the same sense as linoleic acid.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Palmitic acid is a non-essential saturated fatty acid, readily synthesized by the body.

questions.subject: fnd
questions.learning_objective: Identify linoleic acid as a true essential fatty acid, distinct from oleic and palmitic acid (non-essential) and arachidonic acid (conditionally essential, derived from linoleic acid).

questions.title: Cerebroside composition
questions.question: Cerebrosides are glycolipids. What are the compositions of cerebrosides?

options.A: Sphingosine, fatty acids, glycerol, phosphoric acid

explanations.A: Incorrect. This option describes sphingomyelin's composition (which does include phosphoric acid, via a phosphodiester bond) rather than the cerebroside's — cerebrosides contain no phosphate.
explanations.B: Correct. A cerebroside is a glycosphingolipid built from ceramide (sphingosine joined to a fatty acid by an amide bond) with a single sugar — classically galactose — attached to the sphingosine's terminal hydroxyl. It contains no glycerol and no phosphate group, distinguishing it from both sphingomyelin and the glycerophospholipids.
explanations.C: Incorrect. This option substitutes glycerol for sphingosine — but cerebrosides are sphingolipids, built on a sphingosine backbone, not a glycerol backbone.
explanations.D: Incorrect. This option incorrectly adds both glucose and glycerol; the cerebroside's actual composition has only sphingosine, fatty acid and (classically) galactose, with no glycerol.

questions.subject: fnd
questions.learning_objective: State the sphingosine/fatty-acid/galactose composition of a cerebroside, distinguishing it from sphingomyelin's phosphate-containing composition and from glycerol-backbone lipids.

questions.title: Glutathione hydrolytic products
questions.question: Glutathione is one of biologically active peptides. What are the hydrolytic products of glutathione?

explanations.A: Incorrect. Serine is not one of glutathione's three components — the third component is glycine, not serine.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Glutamine, not glutamic acid (glutamate), is substituted here — glutathione's actual first component is glutamic acid.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Taurine is a cysteine-derived compound but is not itself one of glutathione's own hydrolytic products.
explanations.D: Correct. Glutathione is a tripeptide (gamma-glutamylcysteinylglycine) whose complete hydrolysis yields exactly three amino acids: glutamic acid, cysteine and glycine. The cysteine's free thiol group is what gives glutathione its antioxidant, free-radical-scavenging function.

questions.subject: fnd
questions.learning_objective: Name glutamic acid, cysteine and glycine as glutathione's three hydrolytic products, rejecting distractors that substitute serine, glutamine or taurine for one of them.

questions.title: Essential hydroxyl-containing amino acid
questions.question: Which of the following is an essential amino acid that contains OH group?

explanations.A: Incorrect. Valine is essential but has a branched aliphatic side chain, no hydroxyl group.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Tryptophan is essential but has an indole side chain, no hydroxyl group.
explanations.C: Correct. Threonine is one of the essential amino acids and carries a hydroxyl (OH) group on its side chain — alongside serine and tyrosine, which also have an OH group but are not essential in the same sense. Among the essential amino acids specifically, threonine is the classic hydroxyl-bearing one this question is testing.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Phenylalanine is essential but has an aromatic phenyl side chain, no hydroxyl group (its hydroxylated derivative, tyrosine, is non-essential).

questions.subject: fnd
questions.learning_objective: Identify threonine as the essential amino acid bearing a hydroxyl group, distinct from valine, tryptophan and phenylalanine, none of which has a hydroxyl side chain.

questions.title: Protein that binds DNA
questions.question: Which one of the following proteins binds to DNA?

explanations.A: Incorrect. Albumin is a plasma transport protein; it does not bind DNA.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Globulins are a diverse plasma protein family (including antibodies and transport proteins); they do not bind DNA as a defining function.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Keratin is the intermediate filament protein of epithelium, an entirely structural cytoskeletal role unrelated to DNA binding.
explanations.D: Correct. Histones are lysine- and arginine-rich basic proteins that condense DNA into nucleosomes — positively charged proteins that bind the acidic, phosphate-rich DNA electrostatically, forming the first level of chromatin packing.

questions.subject: fnd
questions.learning_objective: Identify histone as the DNA-binding protein among albumin, globulin and keratin.

questions.title: tRNA TψC arm and thymine
questions.question: Which of the following is true about tRNA?

options.A: The specificity of a tRNA for a particular amino acid is contained in its acceptor arm
options.B: T ψ C contains thymine bases
options.C: Acceptor arm at terminal 5' COOH sequence is always CCA
options.D: Each tRNA has an average 275 nucleotide residues

explanations.A: Incorrect. A tRNA's amino-acid specificity is contained in its anticodon, which pairs with the mRNA codon, not in its acceptor arm, which simply carries the activated amino acid regardless of which tRNA it is attached to.
explanations.B: Correct. The TψC arm (T-psi-C loop) of tRNA is named for the three bases characteristically found there — thymine (an unusual base for RNA, more typical of DNA), pseudouridine (ψ) and cytosine. Recognising thymine's presence there is a specific, frequently tested structural exception in an otherwise ribonucleotide molecule.
explanations.C: Incorrect. The acceptor arm's terminal sequence is 3'-CCA-OH, not '5' COOH' as stated here — this option reverses the correct terminus and invents an incorrect chemical group.
explanations.D: Incorrect. An average tRNA is roughly 75 to 90 nucleotides long, not 275 — this option overstates the true length by roughly threefold.

questions.subject: fnd
questions.learning_objective: State that the tRNA TψC arm contains thymine, and correctly reject distractors about acceptor-arm amino-acid specificity, the acceptor arm's terminal sequence, and tRNA's true average length.

questions.title: Extracellular enzyme example
questions.question: Which of the following is an example of an extracellular enzyme?

explanations.A: Incorrect. Lactate dehydrogenase is a cytoplasmic enzyme of glycolysis/gluconeogenesis; it only appears in blood after cell damage, but its normal site of action is intracellular.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Cytochrome oxidase (Complex IV) is a mitochondrial enzyme of the electron transport chain, entirely intracellular.
explanations.C: Correct. Pancreatic lipase is secreted by pancreatic acinar cells into the pancreatic duct and, from there, into the intestinal lumen, where it acts on dietary triglycerides entirely outside any cell — a genuine extracellular enzyme.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Hexokinase is a cytoplasmic enzyme catalysing the first step of glycolysis, an intracellular reaction.

questions.subject: fnd
questions.learning_objective: Identify pancreatic lipase as a genuinely extracellular enzyme, distinct from lactate dehydrogenase, cytochrome oxidase and hexokinase, which all act intracellularly.

questions.title: Non-competitive enzyme inhibition and Vmax
questions.question: In reversible non-competitive enzyme activity inhibition, the inhibitor binds at a site distinct to the substrate binding site. Which of the following is correct concerning it?

options.A: Inhibitor bears structural resemblance to substrate
options.B: Inhibitor lowers the maximum velocity attainable with a given amount of enzyme

explanations.A: Incorrect. Requiring structural resemblance to the substrate is the defining feature of competitive inhibition (which binds the same active site as the substrate), not non-competitive inhibition, which binds elsewhere.
explanations.B: Correct. In reversible non-competitive inhibition, the inhibitor binds a site distinct from the substrate-binding site, effectively removing some active enzyme from the usable pool regardless of substrate concentration — so Vmax falls, and cannot be restored by adding more substrate.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Km is characteristically unchanged in non-competitive inhibition, not increased — an increased Km is the signature of competitive inhibition instead.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Km is not decreased in non-competitive inhibition; it remains unchanged, since the inhibitor does not compete with the substrate for the same binding site.

questions.subject: fnd
questions.learning_objective: State that reversible non-competitive inhibition lowers the maximum velocity (Vmax) attainable with a given amount of enzyme, distinct from the structural-resemblance-to-substrate feature of competitive inhibition.

questions.title: Vitamin A deficiency
questions.question: A 21-year-old man suffered from inability to drive at night for 6 months. Clinical examination revealed xerophthalmia and xeroderma. A deficiency of which of the following vitamins is deficient?

explanations.A: Correct. Vitamin A (retinol) is essential for the visual cycle (as 11-cis-retinal, part of rhodopsin) and for epithelial integrity. Its deficiency classically presents with inability to see in dim light (night blindness, from impaired rhodopsin regeneration) progressing to dryness of the conjunctiva/cornea (xerophthalmia) and dryness of the skin (xeroderma) — exactly the triad in this vignette.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Vitamin C deficiency causes scurvy (gum disease, poor wound healing, bruising), not this night-blindness/xerophthalmia/xeroderma triad.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Vitamin D deficiency causes bone-mineralisation defects (rickets in children, osteomalacia in adults), not this visual/epithelial presentation.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Vitamin E deficiency causes neuromuscular findings and hemolytic anemia (notably in premature infants), not this specific triad.

questions.subject: fnd
questions.learning_objective: Recognise the vitamin A deficiency triad — night blindness, xerophthalmia, xeroderma — from a clinical vignette, distinct from vitamin C, D and E deficiency presentations.

questions.title: Vitamin K deficiency in the newborn
questions.question: A 2-day-neonate suffered from bleeding from the umbilicus and hemorrhagic tendency. He was born at home and didn't receive any medication since birth. Laboratory investigations showed prolongation of clotting time. Which of the following vitamins is deficient?

explanations.A: Incorrect. Pyridoxine (B6) deficiency causes peripheral neuropathy, dermatitis and sideroblastic anemia, not this coagulation abnormality.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Riboflavin (B2) deficiency causes mucocutaneous findings (cheilosis, glossitis), not a clotting-time abnormality.
explanations.C: Correct. Vitamin K is required for gamma-carboxylation of clotting factors II, VII, IX and X in the liver; newborns have low vitamin K stores (poor placental transfer, sterile gut with no bacterial vitamin K synthesis yet, low breast-milk content) and, without prophylaxis, can develop hemorrhagic disease of the newborn — bleeding, classically from the umbilicus, with a prolonged clotting time, exactly as in this vignette.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Vitamin C deficiency causes scurvy, a connective-tissue and capillary fragility disorder, not a clotting-factor-dependent bleeding picture with prolonged clotting time.

questions.subject: fnd
questions.learning_objective: Recognise vitamin K deficiency as the cause of neonatal umbilical bleeding with prolonged clotting time in an unmedicated home birth, distinct from pyridoxine, riboflavin and vitamin C deficiency.

questions.title: Beriberi and vitamin B1
questions.question: Vitamins deficiencies lead to serious illnesses; What is vitamin deficiency cause Beriberi?

explanations.A: Correct. Vitamin B1 (thiamine) is a cofactor (as thiamine pyrophosphate) for several key enzymes (pyruvate dehydrogenase, alpha-ketoglutarate dehydrogenase, transketolase); its deficiency causes beriberi, presenting as either a peripheral neuropathy (dry beriberi) or high-output cardiac failure with edema (wet beriberi).
explanations.B: Incorrect. B2 (riboflavin) deficiency causes ariboflavinosis (cheilosis, glossitis, dermatitis), not beriberi.
explanations.C: Incorrect. B6 (pyridoxine) deficiency causes peripheral neuropathy and dermatitis, a different syndrome from beriberi.
explanations.D: Incorrect. B12 (cobalamin) deficiency causes megaloblastic anemia and neurological findings (subacute combined degeneration), not beriberi.

questions.subject: fnd
questions.learning_objective: Name vitamin B1 (thiamine) as the vitamin whose deficiency causes beriberi, distinct from B2, B6 and B12 deficiency syndromes.

questions.title: Vitamin B12 deficiency on a vegetarian diet
questions.question: A 41-year-old journalist consumes on a vegetarian diet. After two years symptoms of vitamin deficiency develop. Which of the following vitamins is suspected to be deficient?

explanations.A: Incorrect. Thiamine deficiency (beriberi) does not have this same years-long latency from a purely dietary vegetarian cause; thiamine is present in plant foods (whole grains, legumes).
explanations.B: Incorrect. Niacin deficiency (pellagra) is likewise not the classic years-long-latency vegetarian-diet deficiency; niacin is present in many plant foods.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Folate is present in plant foods (leafy greens, legumes), and when folate deficiency does occur it develops over months, not years, since folate's body stores are much smaller than B12's.
explanations.D: Correct. Vitamin B12 (cobalamin) is obtained only from animal-derived foods; a strict vegetarian diet provides essentially none. Because the liver stores several years' worth of B12, deficiency symptoms characteristically take years to appear after dietary B12 intake stops — matching this vignette's two-year vegetarian-diet timeline before symptoms emerge.

questions.subject: fnd
questions.learning_objective: Recognise vitamin B12 deficiency as the vitamin whose deficiency takes years, not months, to manifest on a vegetarian diet, due to large hepatic stores, distinct from thiamine, niacin and folic acid.

questions.title: Folic acid and one-carbon metabolism
questions.question: Folic acid is important for which of the following biochemical processes?

explanations.A: Incorrect. Fatty acid oxidation depends on carnitine and the beta-oxidation enzyme system, not folate.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Fatty acid synthesis depends on acetyl-CoA carboxylase and fatty acid synthase, not folate.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Gluconeogenesis depends on its own dedicated enzyme set (pyruvate carboxylase, PEPCK, fructose-1,6-bisphosphatase, glucose-6-phosphatase), not folate.
explanations.D: Correct. Folic acid, as its coenzyme form tetrahydrofolate, carries and transfers one-carbon units (methyl, methylene, formyl groups) in reactions including purine synthesis, thymidylate (dTMP) synthesis, and methionine regeneration from homocysteine — collectively 'one-carbon metabolism', folate's core biochemical role.

questions.subject: fnd
questions.learning_objective: State that folic acid's core biochemical role is one-carbon metabolism, distinct from fatty acid oxidation, fatty acid synthesis and gluconeogenesis.
